# From Week 2 (cut 2026-10-20) {.center}

The mid-deck recap, cut when the old Part 4 (spurious correlations) was folded into
Part 3. The three-card summary at the end covers it.

# Distributions so far

- A **distribution** describes a number by all the values it could take, not just one.
- **Distributions of data**: how values vary across a population. Center, spread,
  shape. A z-score says where one case sits.
- **Distributions of belief**: how plausible each value of an unknown is. Wide when we
  know little.
- **Correlation** (*r*) and **regression** (β) describe how two variables vary
  together. With standardized data and one predictor, β = *r*.
- β is unknown, so it has a distribution of belief too.

::: {.notes}
- Quick recap before Part 4. Check for questions.
- The thread: every tool so far either describes a distribution (center, spread, shape, r, β) or places a case in one (z-scores), and unknowns get distributions of belief.
- Pivot: these descriptions are real patterns. Next, how real patterns can still mislead.
:::

# From Week 2 (cut 2026-10-26) {.center}

The made-up district opener ("The poor got poorer?": remittances lift families over the
poverty line, and both group averages fall), and two slides that followed the Nepal
earnings puzzle: the 2008 dot plot by education level, and "Counted the same way both
years". The animated reclassification slide replaced them. The R below was in
r/week2.R: to reuse these slides, source it after r/week2.R, and add
`district <- district_summary()` to the setup chunk.

```{r week2-parked-code, eval = FALSE}
# ---- The opening puzzle: the poor got poorer? --------------------------------------

# A made-up district of 10,000 households. Monthly incomes (thousand rupees) follow a
# smooth, right-skewed distribution, split by a poverty line. This year, remittances
# lift the families just under the line (from `from` up to the line) over it: they
# land spread evenly across `land`, depending on how much is sent. Nobody else's
# income changes.
DISTRICT <- list(meanlog = log(30), sdlog = 0.55, line = 20, from = 18, land = c(21, 39))

# The share of households remittances lift over the line
lifted_share <- function(d = DISTRICT) {
  plnorm(d$line, d$meanlog, d$sdlog) - plnorm(d$from, d$meanlog, d$sdlog)
}

# The distribution of income, last year and this year, on a fine grid: the share of
# households per thousand rupees of income
district_curves <- function(d = DISTRICT, to = 400) {
  tibble(x = seq(0.005, to, by = 0.01)) |>
    mutate(
      before = dlnorm(x, d$meanlog, d$sdlog),
      moved = if_else(x >= d$land[1] & x < d$land[2], lifted_share(d) / diff(d$land), 0),
      after = if_else(x >= d$from & x < d$line, 0, before) + moved
    )
}

# Each group's average income and the share of households that are poor, last year and
# this year: before[["poor"]], after[["rich"]], after[["share"]], ...
district_summary <- function(d = DISTRICT) {
  g <- district_curves(d)
  summarize <- function(dens) {
    poor <- g$x < d$line
    c(
      poor = sum(g$x[poor] * dens[poor]) / sum(dens[poor]),
      rich = sum(g$x[!poor] * dens[!poor]) / sum(dens[!poor]),
      all = sum(g$x * dens) / sum(dens),
      share = sum(dens[poor]) / sum(dens)
    )
  }
  list(before = summarize(g$before), after = summarize(g$after))
}

# "The poor got poorer?": a slope chart, last year to this year. Step 1: each group's
# average income last year. 2: this year, both averages fall. 3: fourteen households
# behind them, evenly spread through the distribution, a line each: flat, except the
# ones remittances lifted over the line.
district_slope_plot <- function(step, d = DISTRICT) {
  sm <- district_summary(d)
  groups <- tibble(
    group = c("Not poor", "Poor"),
    before = sm$before[c("rich", "poor")],
    after = sm$after[c("rich", "poor")],
    color = c(BLUE, INK)
  )
  households <- tibble(before = qlnorm((1:14) / 15, d$meanlog, d$sdlog)) |>
    mutate(
      lifted = before >= d$from & before < d$line,
      # where in the landing range: as far along it as they were along the lifted slice
      after = if_else(lifted, d$land[1] + (before - d$from) / (d$line - d$from) * diff(d$land), before)
    ) |>
    filter(before < 70) # the richest few would stretch the axis

  p <- ggplot() +
    scale_x_continuous(
      breaks = 1:2, labels = c("Last year", "This year"),
      limits = c(0.25, 2.55), position = "top"
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 70), breaks = seq(0, 60, 20)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Monthly income (thousand rupees)") +
    theme(
      panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
      axis.text.x.top = element_text(size = 24, face = "bold", color = INK)
    )
  if (step >= 3) {
    p <- p +
      geom_segment(
        data = households,
        aes(x = 1, xend = 2, y = before, yend = after, color = I(if_else(lifted, GREEN, tint(GRAY, 0.55)))),
        linewidth = 0.9
      )
  }
  if (step >= 2) {
    p <- p +
      geom_segment(
        data = groups, aes(x = 1, xend = 2, y = before, yend = after, color = I(color)),
        linewidth = 2.5
      ) +
      geom_point(data = groups, aes(2, after, color = I(color)), size = 7) +
      geom_text(
        data = groups, aes(2, after, label = paste0(fmt(after), "  ▼")),
        hjust = -0.25, size = 9, fontface = "bold", color = RED
      )
  }
  p +
    geom_point(data = groups, aes(1, before, color = I(color)), size = 7) +
    geom_text(
      data = groups,
      aes(1, before, label = paste0(group, "  ", fmt(before)), color = I(color)),
      hjust = 1.12, size = 8, fontface = "bold"
    )
}

# "Why both averages fell": the distribution of income, split at the poverty line into
# the poor and everyone else, with each group's average marked underneath. Step 1: last
# year. 2: the families just under the line, the richest of the poor, get remittances.
# 3: they land just over it, at the bottom of the other group: both averages fall.
poverty_curves_plot <- function(step, d = DISTRICT) {
  g <- district_curves(d, to = 80)
  sm <- district_summary(d)
  now <- if (step >= 3) sm$after else sm$before
  g$y <- if (step >= 3) g$after else g$before
  top <- max(g$before)
  base <- -0.16 * top # room under the axis for the averages

  marks <- tibble(
    x = now[c("poor", "rich")],
    was = sm$before[c("poor", "rich")],
    label = paste("average", fmt(now[c("poor", "rich")])),
    color = c(INK, BLUE)
  )
  w <- 1.4 # half a triangle's width
  triangles <- marks |>
    mutate(id = row_number()) |>
    rowwise() |>
    reframe(id, color, x = x + c(0, -w, w), y = c(-0.012, 0.42, 0.42) * base / 0.42 * 0.5)

  p <- ggplot(g, aes(x)) +
    geom_area(data = filter(g, x < d$line), aes(y = y), fill = tint(INK, 0.45)) +
    geom_area(data = filter(g, x >= d$line), aes(y = y), fill = tint(BLUE, 0.5)) +
    geom_line(aes(y = y), color = INK, linewidth = 0.8)
  if (step == 2) {
    slice <- filter(g, x >= d$from, x < d$line)
    landing <- filter(g, x >= d$land[1], x < d$land[2])
    p <- p +
      geom_area(data = slice, aes(y = before), fill = GREEN) +
      geom_ribbon(data = landing, aes(ymin = before, ymax = before + moved), fill = NA, color = GREEN, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
      annotate(
        "curve", x = (d$from + d$line) / 2, xend = mean(d$land), y = top * 0.75, yend = top * 1.1,
        curvature = -0.35, color = GREEN, linewidth = 1.3, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.12, "inches"), type = "closed")
      ) +
      annotate("text", x = (d$from + d$line) / 2, y = top * 0.82, label = "remittances", color = GREEN, size = 7, fontface = "bold", hjust = 1.05)
  }
  if (step >= 3) {
    p <- p +
      geom_ribbon(
        data = filter(g, moved > 0), aes(ymin = before, ymax = after),
        fill = GREEN
      ) +
      geom_segment(
        data = marks, aes(x = was, xend = x, y = base * 1.6, yend = base * 1.6),
        color = RED, linewidth = 1.3, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.1, "inches"), type = "closed")
      ) +
      geom_text(
        data = marks, aes(x = x, y = base * 1.6, label = paste0("−", fmt(was - x))),
        hjust = 1.3, color = RED, size = 6.5, fontface = "bold"
      ) +
      geom_segment(data = marks, aes(x = was, xend = was, y = 0, yend = base * 0.5), color = GRAY, linetype = "dashed")
  }
  share <- now[["share"]]
  p +
    geom_polygon(data = triangles, aes(x, y, group = id, fill = I(color))) +
    geom_text(data = marks, aes(x, base * 1.05, label = label, color = I(color)), size = 6, fontface = "bold") +
    annotate("segment", x = d$line, xend = d$line, y = base * 0.3, yend = top * 1.25, color = RED, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.1) +
    annotate("text", x = d$line, y = top * 1.31, label = "poverty line", color = RED, size = 6.5) +
    annotate("text", x = 2, y = top * 1.2, label = paste0("Poor: ", round(100 * share), "%"), hjust = 0, size = 7, fontface = "bold", color = INK) +
    annotate("text", x = 79, y = top * 1.2, label = paste0("Not poor: ", round(100 * (1 - share)), "%"), hjust = 1, size = 7, fontface = "bold", color = BLUE) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 80), breaks = seq(0, 80, 10)) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(base * 1.85, top * 1.33), clip = "off") +
    labs(x = "Monthly household income (thousand rupees, made-up)", y = NULL) +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
}

# "Move one group, raise both averages": 2008's paid employees by education level, a
# dot each at its average earnings, sized by how many there are, in two groups with
# each group's average as a line. Step 1: grouped as the ILO's 2008 tables group them.
# 2: grades 11–12, between the two averages. 3: counted as secondary, as in 2017/18.
# Both averages rise (the old ones stay, dashed); all employees' doesn't move.
edu_move_plot <- function(step, levels = nlfs_levels(), groups = nlfs_groups()) {
  coding <- if (step >= 3) "same" else "ilo"
  dots <- levels |>
    filter(year == 2008) |>
    mutate(row = as.integer(level), group = if_else(is_post(isced, year, coding), "post", "secondary"))
  means <- groups |> filter(year == 2008)
  was <- filter(means, coding == "ilo")
  now <- filter(means, coding == !!coding) |>
    left_join(summarize(dots, lo = min(row), hi = max(row), .by = group), by = "group") |>
    mutate(was = was$earnings[match(group, was$group)], color = EDU_COLORS[group])
  everyone <- means$earnings[means$coding == "all"]
  movers <- filter(dots, isced == "5")
  dot_color <- if_else(step >= 2 & dots$isced == "5", GREEN, EDU_COLORS[dots$group])

  p <- ggplot() +
    geom_rect(
      data = now, aes(xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = lo - 0.5, ymax = hi + 0.5, fill = I(tint(color, 0.08)))
    ) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = now$lo[now$group == "post"] - 0.5, color = GRAY, linetype = "dashed")
  if (step >= 3) {
    p <- p +
      geom_segment(
        data = now, aes(x = was, xend = was, y = lo - 0.4, yend = hi + 0.4),
        color = GRAY, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1
      )
  }
  p <- p +
    geom_segment(
      data = now, aes(x = earnings, xend = earnings, y = lo - 0.4, yend = hi + 0.4, color = I(color)),
      linewidth = 2.5
    ) +
    geom_point(data = dots, aes(earnings, row, size = employees, color = I(dot_color)), alpha = 0.85) +
    scale_size_area(max_size = 17, guide = "none")
  if (step == 2) {
    p <- p + annotate(
      "text", x = movers$earnings - 1.6, y = movers$row,
      label = paste0(fmt(round(movers$employees, 0) * 1000, 0), "\nemployees"),
      hjust = 1, lineheight = 0.9, size = 6, color = GREEN, fontface = "bold"
    )
  }
  # Each group's name and average, in its band's free corner: post-secondary top left,
  # secondary or less on the right
  tags <- now |>
    mutate(
      post = group == "post",
      x = if_else(post, 9.8, 49.2),
      y = if_else(post, hi + 0.4, (lo + hi) / 2 + 1),
      hjust = if_else(post, 0, 1),
      label = paste0(if_else(post, "Post-secondary", "Secondary or less"), "\naverage ", fmt(earnings))
    )
  p <- p +
    geom_text(
      data = tags, aes(x, y, label = label, hjust = hjust, color = I(color)),
      vjust = 1, lineheight = 0.95, size = 6.5, fontface = "bold"
    ) +
    annotate(
      "text", x = 49.2, y = 1, label = paste("All employees:", fmt(everyone), "either way"),
      hjust = 1, size = 6, color = GRAY
    )
  if (step >= 3) {
    p <- p + geom_text(
      data = tags, aes(x, y - 1, label = paste("▲", fmt(earnings - was)), hjust = hjust),
      vjust = 1, size = 6.5, fontface = "bold", color = GREEN
    )
  }
  p +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(9.5, 49.5), breaks = seq(10, 50, 10), expand = expansion(0)) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq_along(levels(dots$level)), labels = levels(dots$level), expand = expansion(add = 0.1)) +
    coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
    labs(x = "Monthly earnings in 2008 (thousand rupees)", y = NULL) +
    theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}
```

# The poor got poorer?

_A district of 10,000 households, a year apart._

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.r-stack}
::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{r district-1, opts.label = "puzzle"}
district_slope_plot(1)
```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=1}
```{r district-2, opts.label = "puzzle"}
district_slope_plot(2)
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
```{r district-3, opts.label = "puzzle"}
district_slope_plot(3)
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
Average monthly income, by group (thousand rupees).

- [**Poor households**: [down]{.red}, from `r fmt(district$before[["poor"]])` to
  `r fmt(district$after[["poor"]])`.]{.fragment fragment-index=1}
- [**Everyone else**: [down]{.red} too, from `r fmt(district$before[["rich"]])` to
  `r fmt(district$after[["rich"]])`.]{.fragment fragment-index=1}
- [Each gray line is a household, picked from across the district. None fell. The
  green one rose.]{.fragment fragment-index=2}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3 .big-statement}
Both averages fell.\
No family got poorer.\
Good news or bad?
:::
:::
:::

[A made-up district.]{.source}

::: {.notes}
- Week 1 opened with a claim that sounded wrong and turned out true. This week opens with a puzzle, solved on the next slide.
- Set it up. A district of 10,000 households, one year apart. The government counts a household as poor if its income is below a poverty line. The chart shows each group's average monthly income, in thousands of rupees.
- Click: this year, the average poor household earns less than last year, about 13.8 thousand instead of 15.0. And the average household that isn't poor also earns less: 40.1 instead of 40.9.
- Ask what a newspaper would write. "The poor are getting poorer, and so is everyone else." A minister would be asked to explain.
- Click: the gray lines are households picked from across the district, one line each, from last year's income to this year's. They're flat: their income didn't change at all. One, in green, went up.
- Click: so both averages fell, and no family got poorer. Is this good news or bad? Let the room argue before moving on. Some will guess it's a trick of the numbers. It is, sort of, and the trick is in the groups.
- The district is made up, to keep the mechanism visible. The same thing happens with real data whenever cases cross a line between groups. Two slides on, Nepal's own earnings data does it. Another real example, if asked: from 2000 to 2013, the median US wage fell within every education group (dropouts, high-school graduates, some college, degree holders) while the overall median rose, because millions of people moved up into the better-paid groups (Floyd Norris, New York Times, 2013).
:::

## Why both averages fell

_The district's incomes as a distribution, split at the poverty line._

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.r-stack}
::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{r curves-1, opts.label = "puzzle"}
poverty_curves_plot(1)
```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=1}
```{r curves-2, opts.label = "puzzle"}
poverty_curves_plot(2)
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
```{r curves-3, opts.label = "puzzle"}
poverty_curves_plot(3)
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
- [Remittances lift the families just under the line, the richest of the poor, across
  it.]{.fragment fragment-index=1}
- [The poor lose their right edge: their average falls.]{.fragment fragment-index=2}
- [Everyone else gains households below their average: theirs falls
  too.]{.fragment fragment-index=2}
- [Poverty: [`r pct(district$before[["share"]])` → `r pct(district$after[["share"]])`]{.green}.
  Average income: [up]{.green}.]{.fragment fragment-index=3}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=4 .big-statement}
Both fell because families escaped poverty.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- The puzzle, solved, and our first look at this week's subject: a distribution. The curve shows how the district's incomes spread out: how many households earn each amount. Most earn around 20 to 30 thousand; a long tail earns much more. The dashed red line is the poverty line. Everything to its left, in gray, is "poor": 23% of households. Everything to its right, in blue, is everyone else.
- The triangles are each group's average: the point where that piece of the curve would balance. The poor average about 15 thousand, everyone else about 41.
- Click: remittances reach the families just under the line, in green: the richest of the poor. A son or daughter abroad starts sending money home.
- Click: they cross the line, and land spread across the bottom of the other group (the dashed outline, then the green bump). Now watch the triangles. The poor curve has lost its right edge, its richest households, so its balance point moves left: its average falls. The other curve has gained households below its average, so its balance point moves left too. The dashed gray ticks show where they were.
- Click: the numbers that tell the real story. Poverty fell from 23% to 18% of households, and the district's average income rose. Nobody got poorer.
- Click: both averages fell because families escaped poverty. Good news, reported as bad.
- The general rule: whenever cases cross the line between two groups, both groups' averages can move the same way, even though nobody in either group got worse. Moving up out of the lower group pulls both averages down.
- The deeper point: "poor" and "not poor" are a line someone drew. Draw it somewhere else and you get different averages from the same households. Group averages are only as meaningful as the groups. The whole distribution shows what really happened.
- Remittances are a real part of Nepal's story, but don't claim the national figures behave like this district. Here, by design, remittances reach only the families just under the line. In reality they reach families at every income, and the national averages can go either way. The district illustrates the mechanism; it isn't a model of Nepal's economy.
:::

_2008 only. Each dot is an education level, sized by how many employees have it._


::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
```{r edu-move-3, opts.label = "puzzle"}
edu_move_plot(3)
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
- [[Grades 11–12]{.green}: post-secondary in the 2008 tables, secondary in
  2017/18's, after a 2016 school reform.]{.fragment fragment-index=1}
- [They earn between the two averages.]{.fragment fragment-index=1}
- [Count them as secondary in 2008 too: [both]{.green} averages rise.
  Everyone's: no change.]{.fragment fragment-index=2}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3 .big-statement}
Same people, same pay.\
New label.
:::
:::
:::

[Thousand rupees a month, at 2025/26 prices. Source: ILOSTAT tabulations of the
Nepal Labour Force Survey.]{.source}

::: {.notes}
- 2008 only, no change over time. Each dot is an education level at its average monthly earnings, sized by how many employees have it. The thick lines are each group's average.
- Click: the green dot is grades 11–12, the old Intermediate and Proficiency Certificate. 367,000 employees. In 2008 the ILO coded them as short-cycle tertiary, so they count as post-secondary. In 2017/18 they're coded as secondary. That fits Nepal's 2016 education reform, which made grades 9–12 secondary school.
- Be honest about the source: the ILO doesn't document this change. It's inferred from the ILO's own detailed counts (the short-cycle tertiary code, ISCED 5, appears only in 2008; the post-secondary non-tertiary code, ISCED 4, only in 2017/18) and from the reform.
- Their earnings, about 20 thousand, sit between the two averages: more than the secondary average, less than the post-secondary one.
- Click: count them as secondary in 2008 too. The post-secondary group loses its lowest earners, so its average jumps from 24.2 to 34.8. The secondary group gains people who earn more than its average, so its average rises too, from 14.6 to 15.7. All employees: 17.1, unchanged. Same people, same pay.
- This is the Will Rogers paradox, after his joke that when the Okies left Oklahoma for California, they raised the average intelligence of both states. Medicine has a famous version: better scans move patients with small tumours from "early stage" to "late stage", and survival improves in both stages while no patient lives longer.
- Click: same people, same pay, new label. And on the last slide's puzzle: the 2008 groups had both averages lower than they'd be under the 2017/18 coding, so both groups' growth looked bigger than it was.
:::

## Counted the same way both years

_The same groups, with grades 11–12 counted as secondary in 2008 too._

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.r-stack}
::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{r edu-same-1, opts.label = "puzzle"}
edu_growth_plot(1)
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
```{r edu-same-2, opts.label = "puzzle"}
edu_growth_plot(2)
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
- [**Secondary or less**: `r pct(nlfs_stat(edu, "same", "secondary"))`, not
  `r pct(nlfs_stat(edu, "ilo", "secondary"))`.]{.fragment fragment-index=1}
- [**Post-secondary**: `r pct(nlfs_stat(edu, "same", "post"))`, not
  `r pct(nlfs_stat(edu, "ilo", "post"))`.]{.fragment fragment-index=1}
- [Degree holders: `r pct(nlfs_stat(edu, "same", "post", "share_2008"))` →
  `r pct(nlfs_stat(edu, "same", "post", "share_2017"))` of employees. Their pay
  barely beat prices.]{.fragment fragment-index=2}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3 .big-statement}
Ask who's in\
each group.
:::
:::
:::

[Source: ILOSTAT tabulations of the Nepal Labour Force Survey, 2008 and 2017/18;
deflated with the Nepal Rastra Bank CPI.]{.source}

::: {.notes}
- The fix: draw the groups the same way in both years, with grades 11–12 as secondary.
- Click: the published bars fade, and the arrows show the growth on the consistent definition. Secondary or less: 56%, close to the 67% published. Post-secondary, now degree holders only: 10%, not 58%. All employees: 55%, between the two, as an average should be. No paradox.
- Click: the real story is the opposite of the published one. Degree holders doubled, from 7% to 14% of paid employees, and their real pay barely grew. Everyone else's grew by more than half. Economists call it graduate premium compression; studies of returns to education in Nepal find it too.
- Caveats, if asked: these are survey estimates, so differences of a percent or so are noise. Only two survey rounds have earnings by education (the ILO hasn't tabulated the 1998/99 one). Settling it properly takes the survey's microdata from the National Statistics Office.
- Click: the lesson for the week. An average summarizes a crowd of people, a distribution. Change who's in the crowd and the average changes, even when nobody's situation does. So before comparing averages, ask who's in each group, and look at the whole distribution when you can. That's what the rest of today is about.
:::

# From Week 2 (cut 2026-10-26) {.center}

Part 1 refocused on shapes, with the named numbers as labels on them. The 68–95–99.7
rule became bands on "The Normal distribution". The women's and men's heights gave way
to the "Why two humps?" mystery (children and adults); Part 3's "Do men weigh more?"
now states the height gap itself. Nepal's age histogram (an image, NLSS IV with absent
members counted) was redrawn from datasets/nepal_ages.csv, with Japan beside it. The
image is still in images/week2/population.svg. Their R helpers were removed from
r/week2.R; here they are (the slides also used `h_women` and `h_men`, the women's and
men's mean heights, from the deck's setup chunk):

```{r eval = FALSE}
# "One hump or two?": the women's and men's heights, overlapping, with everyone's
# outline on top
height_sex_plot <- function(howell) {
  means <- howell |>
    group_by(sex) |>
    summarise(height = mean(height))

  ggplot(howell, aes(height)) +
    geom_histogram(
      aes(fill = sex),
      binwidth = 2,
      boundary = 0,
      position = "identity",
      alpha = 0.55,
      color = "white"
    ) +
    geom_freqpoly(binwidth = 2, boundary = 0, color = INK, linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_vline(data = means, aes(xintercept = height, color = sex), linewidth = 1.2) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(female = RED, male = BLUE), name = NULL) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(female = RED, male = BLUE), guide = "none") +
    labs(x = "Height (cm)", y = "Number of adults")
}

# "The 68-95-99.7 rule": the standard Normal with 1, 2 and 3 SD bands shaded
normal_rule_plot <- function() {
  bands <- tibble(k = c(3, 2, 1), fill = c(tint(BLUE, 0.18), tint(BLUE, 0.5), BLUE))
  shading <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(bands)), function(i) {
    stat_function(
      fun = dnorm,
      geom = "area",
      xlim = c(-bands$k[i], bands$k[i]),
      fill = bands$fill[i]
    )
  })

  ggplot() +
    xlim(-4, 4) +
    shading +
    stat_function(fun = dnorm, linewidth = 1.2, color = INK) +
    annotate(
      "text",
      x = 0,
      y = 0.18,
      label = "68%",
      size = 10,
      color = "white",
      fontface = "bold"
    ) +
    annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = 0.04, label = "95%", size = 8, color = INK) +
    annotate("text", x = 2.5, y = 0.015, label = "99.7%", size = 7, color = INK) +
    scale_x_continuous(
      breaks = -3:3,
      labels = c("-3 SD", "-2 SD", "-1 SD", "mean", "+1 SD", "+2 SD", "+3 SD")
    ) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())
}
```

## The 68–95–99.7 rule

```{r normal-rule, fig.height = 5.5}
normal_rule_plot()
```

- For a Normal distribution, about **68%** of cases fall within 1 SD of the mean, and
  **95%** within 2 SD.
- [Check: `r fmt(100 * mean(abs(howell$z_height) < 1), 0)`% of !Kung adults are within
  1 SD of the average height, and `r fmt(100 * mean(abs(howell$z_height) < 2), 0)`%
  within 2 SD.]{.fragment}

::: {.notes}
- For a Normal distribution: about 68% of cases within 1 SD, 95% within 2 SD, 99.7% within 3 SD.
- Click: check it against the !Kung data. It's close. That's a good habit: check a rule of thumb against your actual data.
- "Within 2 SD" comes back in Part 2: it's how we'll say how sure we are.
:::

## One hump or two?

_One bell fits everyone. But inside it, the !Kung heights are two crowds._

```{r height-sex, fig.height = 5.4}
height_sex_plot(howell)
```

::: {.fragment}
Women average `r fmt(h_women)` cm, men `r fmt(h_men)` cm. But the crowds overlap: [plenty
of women are taller than plenty of men]{.blue}. (Hold on to this. It comes back.)
:::

::: {.notes}
- A turn after the Normal: one bell fit everyone, but this one distribution is really two, women and men. The dashed line is everyone; the colors are the two groups inside it.
- Each crowd is roughly a bell. They overlap so much that together they still look like one hump. Mean and SD described the whole crowd well, and hid what's inside it.
- Click: the men are about 11 cm taller on average. But look at the overlap. Many women are taller than many men. "Men are taller" is a statement about two distributions, not about every man and every woman.
- Flag it: this comes back at the end of Part 3. Men are also heavier. The question there is whether that's because they're men or because they're taller.
:::

## A shape tells a story
<!-- TODO: Add NLSS age data. Why the bumps? -->
![Population of Nepal](images/week2/population.svg){width="60%" fig-align="center"}

::: {.fragment .big-statement}
An average describes the crowd.\
The distribution describes everyone in it.
:::

::: {.notes}
- A familiar population distribution: Nepal's age pyramid. Ask: what do you notice? Why the bumps?
- Likely discussion points: the base is narrowing because birth rates have fallen a lot. And there are fewer men than women in the working ages, because so many men work abroad. Let students propose these.
- The point is that a distribution's shape carries history. A single number, the average age, would hide all of it.
:::

# From Week 2 (cut 2026-10-26, Part 1's ending) {.center}

"Why two humps?": the weights of everyone Howell counted, children too, ending Part 1.
Cut because the deck works with the adults only. To reuse it, add
`kung_all <- load_howell(adults = FALSE)` to the setup chunk and source the R below
after r/week2.R (it was there; the "puzzle" figure size still is).

```{r eval = FALSE}
# "Why two humps?": the weights of everyone in Howell's census. by_generation = TRUE
# colors children (under 18, light blue) and adults, labels each hump, and marks
# everyone's mean weight, which falls between them.
generation_plot <- function(kung, by_generation = FALSE) {
  kung <- kung |>
    mutate(generation = factor(if_else(age < 18, "children", "adults"), c("children", "adults")))
  humps <- kung |>
    group_by(generation) |>
    summarise(weight = median(weight), n = n()) |>
    mutate(label = paste0(generation, " (", n, ")"))
  colors <- c(children = tint(BLUE, 0.5), adults = BLUE)

  p <- ggplot(kung, aes(weight)) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
    labs(x = "Weight (kg)", y = "Number of people")
  if (!by_generation) {
    return(p + geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, boundary = 0, fill = GRAY, color = "white"))
  }
  p +
    geom_histogram(
      aes(fill = generation),
      binwidth = 2,
      boundary = 0,
      color = "white",
      show.legend = FALSE
    ) +
    geom_text(
      data = humps,
      aes(x = weight, y = Inf, label = label, color = generation),
      vjust = 1.5,
      size = 8,
      fontface = "bold",
      show.legend = FALSE
    ) +
    value_marker(
      mean(kung$weight),
      paste0("mean = ", fmt(mean(kung$weight)), " kg"),
      RED,
      vjust = 4,
      left = TRUE
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = colors) +
    scale_color_manual(values = colors)
}
```

## Why two humps?

_Howell counted everyone, children too: the weights of all `r nrow(kung_all)` people._

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.r-stack}
::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{r generations, opts.label = "puzzle"}
generation_plot(kung_all)
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
```{r generations-split, opts.label = "puzzle"}
generation_plot(kung_all, by_generation = TRUE)
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
**Two generations.** Children and adults are two crowds, each with its own hump.

The average weight, `r fmt(mean(kung_all$weight))` kg, falls between them. It describes
almost nobody.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- A mystery to end the part. So far, only adults. Howell counted everyone, children too: here are all 544 weights. Two humps, about 17 kg and 45 kg (the medians). Ask: why? Let the room guess before clicking.
- Likely guesses: men and women, after the heights (no: here they overlap within the right hump), rich and poor, two villages. Take a few.
- Click: two generations. Children (under 18, light blue) and adults. Each is its own crowd with its own hump, and the full shape is the two added together.
- The red line: everyone's average weight, about 36 kg, sits in the valley between the humps. Hardly anyone weighs that. An average of a two-humped shape describes almost nobody.
- This is the opening puzzle again, from the other side: an average depends on who's in the crowd.
:::

# From Week 2 (cut 2026-11-13) {.center}

The sampling slides between "How old is he?" and the Galton board: the sample-mean widget
(js/sample-mean.js, _includes/week2/sample-mean.md; it needs the deck's adults-data
block, `adults_widget_data(adults)`), the "Two spreads" table, and the "Population or
certainty?" cards. Too much for this unit; "Ask the room" (js/guess-room.js) replaced
them. The R below was in r/week2.R: to reuse "Two spreads", source it after r/week2.R
and add `spreads <- two_spreads(adults)` to the setup chunk.

```{r week2-parked-spreads, eval = FALSE}
# "Two spreads": for each number of adults measured, how far most adults are from the
# average (2 SD), and how far off our estimate of the average could be (2 SD / √n,
# the 95% width of the certainty distribution with a flat prior)
two_spreads <- function(adults, sizes = c(5, 20, 100, nrow(adults))) {
  s <- sd(adults$height)
  tibble(
    n = sizes,
    population = 2 * s,
    certainty = 2 * s / sqrt(sizes)
  )
}
```

## How sure can a few people make us?

_Pretend these `r nrow(adults)` adults are everyone. We can only afford to measure a few._

{{< include _includes/week2/sample-mean.md >}}

::: {.notes}
- The key slide of Part 2: the two kinds side by side, on one axis.
- Set it up: pretend these 5,290 adults are everyone, and we can only afford to measure a few. What's the average height?
- Start with 5. The top shows the five people we measured (blue dots), against everyone (gray). That's a population distribution: how the people we measured vary. The bottom shows how sure we are about the average height: a certainty distribution.
- Click "Measure new people" a few times. Each sample gives a slightly different guess, and the green curve jumps around. The old curves stay behind, faint. The curve is honest: it's about as wide as the jumps.
- Now 20, then 100. Ask them to watch both rows. The dots on top spread just as wide: people are as different as ever. The green curve gets narrow, fast.
- Tick "Show everyone's average." With 100 people, the curve sits right on it.
- If someone asks how the green curve is made: it's the posterior for the average with a flat prior, a Normal centered on the sample's average with spread SD / √n. They don't need the formula; the next slide has the numbers.
:::

## Two spreads

_If we measured n adults, from a much bigger population:_

| Adults measured | [Most adults are within]{.blue} | [95% sure the average is within]{.green} |
|--:|--:|--:|
| `r spreads$n[1]` | ± `r fmt(spreads$population[1])` cm | ± `r fmt(spreads$certainty[1])` cm |
| `r spreads$n[2]` | ± `r fmt(spreads$population[2])` cm | ± `r fmt(spreads$certainty[2])` cm |
| `r spreads$n[3]` | ± `r fmt(spreads$population[3])` cm | ± `r fmt(spreads$certainty[3])` cm |
| `r spreads$n[4]` | ± `r fmt(spreads$population[4])` cm | ± `r fmt(spreads$certainty[4])` cm |

::: {.fragment}
More data doesn't make people any less different. [It makes us more sure.]{.green}
:::

::: {.fragment .big-statement}
Variation is in the world.\
Uncertainty is in us.
:::

::: {.notes}
- The widget's lesson in numbers. Same population, different sample sizes.
- The blue column never changes: most adults are within about 16 cm of average, however many we measure. That's the population distribution.
- The green column shrinks: with 5 people we're 95% sure the average is within about 7 cm; with 5,290, within about a quarter of a centimeter. That's the certainty distribution.
- The width shrinks with the square root of the number of people: four times the data halves the uncertainty. Mention it, don't derive it.
- Click: more data doesn't make people less different. It makes us more sure.
- Click: the line to remember, and a callback to Week 1's "the uncertainty is in us." Variation is a fact about the world: people really differ. Uncertainty is a fact about us: what we know. Statistics needs both, and confusing them is one of the most common mistakes in reading research.
:::

## Population or certainty?

::: {.kinds}
::: {.kind .kind-population}
[Population distributions]{.kind-title}

How a quantity **varies across cases**. Many cases, each with its own value.

- Heights of the adults in a village
- Prices of houses sold last year
- Ages of everyone in Nepal
:::

::: {.kind .kind-certainty}
[Certainty distributions]{.kind-title}

How **plausible** each value of an unknown is. One true value; we're unsure which.

- The mayor's share of the vote (Week 1)
- The age of the man in the photo
- The average height of all Nepali adults
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
Quick test: [many cases that really differ]{.blue}, or [one answer we're unsure
about]{.green}? Same shapes, same vocabulary, different questions.
:::

::: {.notes}
- An important distinction that trips people up later. Population distributions describe how a quantity varies across real cases. Certainty distributions describe how plausible each value of an unknown is. There's one true value; we just don't know it.
- Click: the quick test. Many cases that really differ, or one answer we're unsure about? Try it on the examples on the cards, then on a few of the students' own.
- Same shapes, same vocabulary, same math. That's convenient, and also why they get confused.
- Part 3 needs both: a pattern in the data, and how sure we are about it.
- Before Part 3: the shapes themselves. Same shapes for both kinds, so this is the place to name them, starting with where a shape comes from: the Galton board.
:::
